<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-structured cases, but the debate ultimately turned on whether the motion's "genuinely voluntary/realistic alternatives" gate is actually administrable. CON's core move—that ministerial-exception doctrine already shields religious institutions from judicial scrutiny, so the gate becomes institutional self-certification exactly where it matters (children, thin labor markets)—was pressed hard and specifically in the Pressure Questions round. PRO's best counter ("you cannot defeat a conditional permission by describing conditions it denies") was a genuinely sharp logical move, but when pushed to name the actual adjudicator, PRO could only offer "whatever legislature and court structure the proposition presupposes"—an assertion, not a mechanism. CON's closing exploited that gap decisively and, because CON spoke last, got the final, uncontested word on the debate's most load-bearing dispute. PRO did land a strong, unanswered point of its own late (the parental-consent-is-ubiquitous analogy), but CON's mechanism critique bites at the very feasibility of the motion as a workable rule, making it the more consequential unresolved issue. PRO's Rebuttal 2 was also clipped for exceeding the word limit, a real execution cost that cut off its final elaboration. On balance, CON's practical administrability attack proved more durable than PRO's principled defense of the conditional permission.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's ministerial-exception/administrability challenge (A2.3, sharpened in A3.1 and driven home in A5.1-A5.2) versus PRO's vague "whatever legislature and court structure" answer (B4.1)—CON's unanswered final exploitation of that vagueness was the debate's most decisive exchange.</best_rebuttal>
